1.title: Governing the Design and Build
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Governing the Design and Build. This opens domain three, which follows an A I system through development. Competency A covers the first stage: from the business case to the documented design. It is where most risks can still be designed out.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Set out the business context and use case for an A I system. Carry out or review an impact assessment. Apply policies, best practices and ethics to design and build. Identify and manage risks with matrices, hierarchies, benchmarks and pilots. And document the design and build to show compliance and manage risk.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Ratio of 0.68 Before Launch
1.text: At Helios, Lucia Moreno wants the hiring tool live for the next campaign. Daniel Osei, Head of Data Science, runs the impact assessment, and the result is clear: the tool selects women at sixty-eight percent of the rate of men, an impact ratio of zero point six eight. That is below the usual zero point eight rule-of-thumb threshold. Samira Haddad asks: approve with conditions, fix first, or stop?

1.title: The Business Context and the Use Case
1.text: Start with the use case. Define the purpose and objectives: the problem, and the decision the system will support. Define the users and the affected people: who operates it, and who is subject to its outputs. Define benefits and success criteria, including harm limits. Define constraints and risk tolerance. Define the legal and ethical context. And define alternatives, including a non-A I option. Exam tip: governance starts before design. With no clear purpose, there is no meaningful risk assessment.

1.title: Is AI the Right Tool?
1.text: Is A I the right tool? State the problem before the solution. List alternatives, including rules, process change or a simpler method. Compare benefit, cost and risk. N I S T, in Manage two point one, asks users to weigh viable non-A I alternatives. Then decide: go, no-go, or go with conditions. The mapping work should give enough context for an initial go or no-go decision. Record the reasoning. Exam tip: if a simpler method meets the need with less risk, the governance answer may be not to use A I.

1.title: Approving the Use Case: Gate, Owner and Conditions
1.text: A use case passes the intake gate from module three, with a named business owner, a risk tier and the required sign-offs. At Helios, Lucia Moreno owns the hiring tool, and the committee tiers it high-risk and asks for an impact assessment first. Approval can carry conditions: tests that must pass, controls that must exist, a review date. The approval is recorded with the assumptions it rests on. If the context changes, the use case is re-approved. Exam tip: conditions must be specific, owned and checked.

1.title: Impact Assessments Compared
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Four assessments overlap. A data protection impact assessment, under G D P R Article thirty-five, looks at risk to people's rights from processing personal data, before processing likely to be high risk. A fundamental rights impact assessment, under A I Act Article twenty-seven, is for certain deployers of high-risk systems, before first use, and can cross-refer to a D P I A. An A I system impact assessment, as I S O forty-two thousand and five describes, looks at effects on individuals and society across the life cycle. An algorithmic impact assessment looks at the effects of automated decisions. Do the work once, and cross-reference it.

1.title: Performing an AI Impact Assessment
1.text: How do you perform an impact assessment? Scope the system, with its intended and foreseeable uses. Identify the people and groups affected, including vulnerable groups. Analyze benefits and harms: likelihood, severity and bias metrics. Set mitigations with owners and dates. Approve with conditions, signed by the accountable owner. And monitor and reassess when anything material changes. Exam tip: the point of the assessment is to inform a decision, so its output is a recommendation with conditions.

1.title: Measuring Impact: The Impact Ratio at Helios
1.text: The impact ratio is the selection rate of one group divided by the rate of the highest group. Before the fix, women were selected at sixty-eight percent of the rate of men, a ratio of zero point six eight, below zero point eight. After the fix, the ratio is zero point nine one, above the threshold. A ratio above zero point eight does not prove the tool is lawful, as we saw in module five. It removes the red flag, and testing continues. Use several metrics, because no single number captures fairness. Exam tip: under zero point eight means investigate.

1.title: Acting on the Findings
1.text: What do you do with the finding? Find the cause: biased training data, a proxy feature, an unsuitable threshold, or a flawed label. Mitigate: remove or rebalance features, re-weight data, adjust thresholds, add human review, or change the design. Retest on fresh data and record the result. Decide with the accountable owner: approve with conditions, send back, or stop. At Helios, the team removes proxy features and recalibrates, the ratio becomes zero point nine one, and launch is approved with monitoring. Exam tip: an assessment that finds a problem is a success.

1.title: Governance by Design: The Design Stages
1.text: Apply policy, best practice and ethics at each design step. Purpose and requirements. Data analysis. Architecture and model selection. Human oversight. Metrics and thresholds. Stakeholder engagement and feedback. And operational controls. Each step has a decision and a record. Late fixes cost more, so design in fairness, explainability, privacy and safety from the start. Exam tip: questions about design ask which control belongs at which step.

1.title: Requirements Gathering and Model Selection
1.text: Requirements include functional ones, what the system must do, and responsible-A I ones: fairness targets, explainability level, privacy and security needs, safety and reliability limits, and oversight points. Requirements are testable and traceable to the use case and the risks. Data analysis checks quality, balance and fit before choosing a model. Model selection weighs accuracy, interpretability, data needs, cost, security, and the choice to build, buy or fine-tune. Record the options considered, and why one was chosen. Exam tip: the most accurate model is not automatically the right one.

1.title: Designing Human Oversight
1.text: Three modes of human oversight. In the loop: a person approves each decision, which fits high-stakes individual decisions. On the loop: a person monitors and can intervene, which fits high-volume, lower-stakes work. In command: a person decides whether and how the system is used. Whatever the mode, design time, information, training and authority to override, as module six described under Article fourteen. Guard against automation bias by showing reasons and uncertainty, and log overrides. At Helios, a recruiter reviews every rejection the tool recommends. Exam tip: design the override.

1.title: Metrics and Thresholds
1.text: Choose metrics of several kinds. Performance: accuracy, precision, recall and error rates. Fairness: selection rates, the impact ratio, and error rates by group. Robustness and safety: performance on unusual or adversarial inputs. Explainability: whether reasons can be given to users. Set the thresholds before testing: the acceptance criteria for launch and for later monitoring. The A I Act asks for testing before market placement against predefined metrics and probabilistic thresholds, in Article nine. Trade-offs between metrics are decided by the owner, openly. Exam tip: set thresholds first.

1.title: Stakeholder Engagement, Feedback and Operational Controls
1.text: Engage stakeholders early and repeatedly: users, affected groups, legal, privacy, security and the business. Collect feedback in design reviews and pilots, and record what changed because of it. Design in operational controls: access control, logging, monitoring hooks, change management, and a way to pause or stop. Use security by design, with threat modeling and protection of the data and the model. And hand off operating instructions to the deployer. Exam tip: a system that cannot be logged, monitored or stopped was not designed for governance.

2.title: Internal and External Risk Factors
2.text: Now risk. Internal factors include data quality and bias, model choice and complexity, skills and capacity, and process and approval gaps. External factors include laws and regulators, vendors and the supply chain, attackers and misuse, and social and market context. Risks interact: a weak vendor and poor data can combine. And identify risks to people as well as to the organization. Exam tip: a complete risk review looks both inward and outward.

2.title: The Probability and Severity Harms Matrix
2.text: The probability and severity harms matrix rates each risk on two axes. High probability and high severity come first. Low and low can be accepted or monitored. Consider severity to people, such as rights, safety and livelihood, not only cost. Low-probability, high-severity harms still need controls. At Helios, a biased ranking is medium probability and high severity, so it gets the strongest controls. Exam tip: a matrix ranks risks. The owner sets the risk tolerance.

2.title: The Risk Mitigation Hierarchy
2.text: The risk mitigation hierarchy has an order of preference. First, eliminate the risk through design: remove the feature, the data or the use. Second, mitigate and control: technical safeguards, thresholds, human oversight. Third, inform and train: instructions, warnings and deployer training. Then judge the residual risk acceptable, documented and approved. The A I Act's risk management duty states the same order, in Article nine. Exam tip: a warning or training is the weakest answer when the risk can be designed out.

2.title: Stakeholder Mapping, Use-Case Evaluation and Benchmarking
2.text: Three more tools. Stakeholder mapping lists everyone affected or interested, their influence and stake, and how each will be consulted. Use-case evaluation tests the use case against ethics, law and risk tolerance, and re-evaluates it when it changes. Benchmarking compares performance and risk with standard test sets, similar systems and human baselines. Add internal and external review, with a second pair of eyes from legal, security and independent experts, and record findings in the risk register with owners. Exam tip: mapping the people affected finds harms a team would otherwise miss.

2.title: Pre-Deployment Pilots and Testing
2.text: Before deployment, run pilots and tests. A pilot runs the system on a limited scale to learn before full launch. Shadow mode runs the system without acting, and compares its outputs with human decisions. A phased rollout starts with a small group, then widens, with stop criteria. Testing covers performance, fairness, robustness, security and red-team exercises. Go or no-go criteria are set in advance, and the decision is recorded. The A I Act allows testing in real-world conditions under defined safeguards, in Articles nine and sixty. Exam tip: a pilot has exit criteria.

2.title: Documenting the Design and Build
2.text: Document the design and build to show compliance and manage risk. Auditors, regulators and later teams rely on it. Keep the use case and approval, the impact assessment, the requirements, the design decisions and alternatives, the risk register, the data sources, the test plan and results, and the approvals and versions. Keep it version-controlled, dated and owned. Write it as you go, because reconstructing it later is unreliable. At Helios, it is the file the committee reviews at the launch gate. Exam tip: if it is not documented, an auditor cannot tell whether it was done.

2.title: Documentation for Compliance: Annex IV and Model Records
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The A I Act's technical documentation, in Article eleven and Annex four, is a good model for a high-risk design record. Annex four covers a general description, and the development process: methods, design specifications and trade-offs, architecture, data requirements, the human oversight assessment, pre-determined changes, validation and testing with metrics, and cybersecurity. It also covers monitoring and control, justification of metrics, the risk management system, lifecycle changes, standards applied, the declaration of conformity, and the post-market monitoring plan. Testing logs are dated and signed. Exam tip: documentation is continuing.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Use case: define purpose, users, benefits, constraints and alternatives, and approve with conditions. Impact assessment: the D P I A, the rights assessment and the A I impact assessment overlap; scope, affected people, benefits and harms, mitigation, approval and monitoring; a ratio under zero point eight means investigate. Design: requirements, model selection, oversight, thresholds set first, feedback and operational controls. Risk: factors, matrix, hierarchy, mapping, benchmarking and pilots. Records: a version-controlled design record, modeled on Annex four.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Lucia Moreno asks what must be settled about the business context before the hiring tool is designed. Which set is the best answer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A use case defines the purpose, the users and affected people, the benefits and success criteria, the constraints, and the alternatives, including a non-A I option.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Before launch, Helios's hiring tool selects women at sixty-eight percent of the rate of men. What should Helios conclude and do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. A ratio of zero point six eight is below zero point eight, so it is a red flag. Find the cause, mitigate, retest and decide before launch, and keep the assessment on file.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which two statements about impact assessments are correct? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and E. Article thirty-five requires a D P I A for processing likely to be high risk, and the A I Act lets a deployer's fundamental rights impact assessment cross-refer to a D P I A. An A I impact assessment does not replace a D P I A, and I S O forty-two thousand and five is guidance.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A team is designing a hiring tool. Which two practices best apply governance to the design stage? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Oversight must be designed with real authority to override, and thresholds are set before testing so results cannot move the goalposts. Choosing size over explainability, collecting everything, and skipping feedback work against governance.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. On a probability and severity harms matrix, which risk should the team treat first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The matrix ranks risks by probability and severity, so a high-probability, high-severity risk to people takes priority. Low and low can be accepted or monitored.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. During design review, a team finds a feature that can produce harmful outputs. Under the risk mitigation hierarchy, which response is the most preferred? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The hierarchy prefers eliminating the risk through design, then mitigation and control, then information and training. Removing the cause beats a warning, training or an alert.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Which design-stage record best helps show compliance and manage risk for a high-risk system? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A dated, owned and version-controlled record of the use case, assessment, requirements, alternatives, risks, tests and approvals shows what was done and why. Informal or after-the-fact records cannot do that reliably.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: D. Question two: C. Question three: C and E. Question four: B and D. Question five: A. Question six: D. Question seven: B. That completes Module eight. Next, Module nine covers governing data, training and testing.
